title: Van der Waerden Colorings
origin: Van der Waerden's theorem (1927) states that for any positive integers r and k, there exists a smallest integer W(r,k) such that any r-coloring of {1, ..., W(r,k)} contains a monochromatic arithmetic progression of length k. Despite nearly a century of work, exact values of W(r,k) are known for only a handful of cases. For 2 colors (r=2), we know W(2,3)=9, W(2,4)=35, W(2,5)=178, and W(2,6)=1132. For k>=7, only lower bounds from computer search are known: W(2,7) > 3703 and W(2,8) > 11495, established by SAT-based constructions from Herwig, Heule, and collaborators in the mid-2000s. These bounds have not been improved in nearly two decades. Beating them with a new construction would be a notable result in additive combinatorics.
instance: Fix k in {7, 8}. A submission is a 2-coloring of the integers {1, 2, ..., N}, represented as a binary string or array of length N (where each entry is 0 or 1). The goal is to maximize N subject to the constraint that there is no monochromatic arithmetic progression of length k. That is, for every arithmetic progression a, a+d, a+2d, ..., a+(k-1)d contained in {1,...,N}, at least two of these positions must have different colors.

scoring.summary: Primary score is the length N of the coloring. Secondary score is the number of monochromatic k-APs (for soft progress when no AP-free coloring exists at that N).

metrics.name: Coloring length N
metrics.description: The length of the submitted AP-free coloring. The primary metric: larger is better. Current targets: N > 3703 for k=7, N > 11495 for k=8.

metrics.name: Monochromatic k-AP count
metrics.description: For submissions that are not perfectly AP-free, the number of monochromatic k-APs present. Used as a secondary metric: fewer is better. A count of 0 means a valid, AP-free coloring.

metrics.name: Target k
metrics.description: Longer progressions (k=8) are harder to avoid, so improvements for k=8 are weighted more heavily than for k=7.

scoring.note: Any valid AP-free coloring is accepted and scored by its length. Even matching the current records (3703 for k=7, 11495 for k=8) is meaningful, as independent constructions often reveal new structural insights.

warmup.title: Warm-up: W(2,3) = 9
warmup.body: Find a 2-coloring of {1,...,8} with no monochromatic 3-term arithmetic progression. One solution: [0,1,1,0,0,1,1,0]. Check: the 3-APs in {1,...,8} include (1,2,3), (2,4,6), (1,4,7), etc. For each, verify that not all three positions share the same color. No valid 2-coloring of {1,...,9} exists with no monochromatic 3-AP, which is why W(2,3) = 9.

verification: For each submission with coloring c[1..N] and target k: enumerate all arithmetic progressions of length k within {1,...,N}. For each starting position a and common difference d (where a + (k-1)*d <= N), check whether c[a], c[a+d], ..., c[a+(k-1)*d] are all the same color. If any such monochromatic progression is found, it is counted as a violation. A coloring with 0 violations is valid. Runs in O(N^2/k) time; for N in the range 5,000-50,000, this completes in well under a second in optimized code.

bounds.label: Exact values
bounds.name: W(2,k) for small k
bounds.formula: W(2,3) = 9, W(2,4) = 35, W(2,5) = 178, W(2,6) = 1132. Proven by exhaustive computation.

bounds.label: Lower bound k=7
bounds.name: W(2,7) > 3703
bounds.formula: Established by SAT-based construction (Herwig, Heule, van Lambalgen, van Maaren, 2007). No improvement since.

bounds.label: Lower bound k=8
bounds.name: W(2,8) > 11495
bounds.formula: Established by SAT-based construction. No improvement since mid-2000s.

bounds.label: Asymptotic
bounds.name: W(2,k) grows very fast
bounds.formula: Gowers (2001) proved W(2,k) <= 2^(2^(2^(2^(2^(k+9))))). The true growth rate is between polynomial towers and the Ackermann function.

bounds.label: Formal math
bounds.name: Lean formalization exists
bounds.formula: DeepMind Formal Conjectures issue #2286 formalizes van der Waerden numbers in Lean 4, so a Lean proof certificate is an alternative submission format.

leaderboard.note: Two-color van der Waerden numbers W(2,k). Values marked 'exact' are proven; 'lower bound' means only the best construction is known.

rows.note: TARGET: Herwig et al., SAT construction

suggestedApproach.title: Verify the warm-up
suggestedApproach.body: Check that [0,1,1,0,0,1,1,0] has no monochromatic 3-AP in {1,...,8}. Then try to extend it to length 9. You will fail, confirming W(2,3) = 9.

suggestedApproach.title: SAT-based search
suggestedApproach.body: Encode the problem as a SAT instance: N binary variables (the coloring), with clauses forbidding each monochromatic k-AP. Use a modern SAT solver (CaDiCaL, Kissat) and incrementally extend N until no satisfying assignment exists.

suggestedApproach.title: Greedy extension with backtracking
suggestedApproach.body: Start from a short AP-free coloring and extend one position at a time. When stuck (both colors create a monochromatic k-AP), backtrack. Combine with look-ahead to prune unpromising branches.

suggestedApproach.title: Cyclic and algebraic constructions
suggestedApproach.body: Many strong colorings have algebraic structure (e.g., based on quadratic residues mod a prime). Search over primes p and residue-based coloring rules to generate long AP-free colorings.

suggestedApproach.title: Reinforcement learning
suggestedApproach.body: Train an RL agent to assign colors one position at a time, rewarding longer AP-free prefixes. The state space is the current partial coloring and the set of almost-monochromatic progressions.

agentPrompt: I want you to find a 2-coloring of {1,...,N} with no monochromatic arithmetic progression of length 7, for N as large as possible. The current record is N = 3703. A coloring is a binary array c[1..N] where each entry is 0 or 1. For it to be valid, there must be no positions a, a+d, a+2d, a+3d, a+4d, a+5d, a+6d (all in {1..N}) where all 7 values have the same color. Strategy: try algebraic constructions based on quadratic residues modulo a prime p. For a prime p, color position i as 0 if i mod p is a quadratic residue, 1 otherwise. Search over primes p near 3700 and beyond. Also try SAT-based search: encode the constraints as a SAT instance and use CaDiCaL or Kissat. Report the coloring as a JSON array of 0s and 1s.
